questions.prompt: Which TLS 1.3 feature allows a client to send application data before completing the new handshake?
wrong: CertificateVerify
KeyUpdate
HelloRetryRequest

questions.prompt: Why can accepted TLS 1.3 0-RTT application data have a replay risk?
questions.correct: It can be sent using PSK-derived early keys before the fresh ServerHello contributes to the handshake
wrong: Every 0-RTT record is plaintext
TLS disables authentication whenever early data is used
The server always reuses the same certificate signature

questions.prompt: An application accepts TLS 1.3 0-RTT requests. Which request is the more dangerous candidate to permit without application-level replay protection?
wrong: Retrieve a static public help page
Fetch a cacheable public image
Read a public status description

questions.prompt: A resumed TLS 1.3 session authenticates the client via a valid PSK. Does that, by itself, eliminate replay risk for accepted 0-RTT requests?
questions.correct: No; PSK authentication alone does not make early data replay-safe
wrong: Yes; every authenticated TLS record is inherently single-use
Yes; 0-RTT uses the fresh ServerHello random in its keys
No; because PSKs cannot authenticate anything in TLS 1.3

questions.prompt: What key-establishment technique is used to obtain forward secrecy in a typical TLS 1.3 full handshake?
wrong: A static server RSA key exchange
An HTTP redirect
A checksum of the server certificate

questions.prompt: For TLS 1.3 PSK resumption, which mode adds fresh Diffie-Hellman to provide forward secrecy for handshake traffic keys?
wrong: psk_ke
No key-exchange mode can use DHE with PSK
Renegotiation using TLS 1.2

questions.prompt: A TLS 1.3 full handshake used ephemeral (EC)DHE, and its ephemeral secrets were erased. An attacker later steals the server's certificate signing key. What follows for the recorded past traffic?
questions.correct: The signing-key theft alone does not reveal the erased ephemeral shared secret
wrong: All recorded traffic is decrypted automatically
The client must retroactively resend its traffic under a new certificate
The server's public certificate contains the traffic secret

questions.prompt: A TLS 1.3 resumed handshake uses PSK plus DHE for 1-RTT keys and also accepts 0-RTT. Which statement correctly distinguishes their protection?
questions.correct: Fresh DHE can protect 1-RTT traffic, but 0-RTT early data lacks the same forward secrecy
wrong: Both 0-RTT and 1-RTT use the fresh DHE secret from the start
Neither 0-RTT nor 1-RTT can ever use forward secrecy
Early data is more forward-secret than later application data

questions.prompt: In a certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 server handshake, which message proves possession of the private key corresponding to the certificate?
wrong: ClientHello
ChangeCipherSpec
NewSessionTicket

questions.prompt: What does the TLS 1.3 Finished message primarily authenticate?
questions.correct: The handshake transcript using a key derived from the negotiated handshake secrets
wrong: Only the DNS A record of the server
The server's operating-system patch level
The client's HTTP request body before it exists

questions.prompt: A server sends a syntactically valid certificate chain, but the leaf certificate does not match the requested hostname. How should a standard HTTPS client validating server identity treat it?
questions.correct: Reject the identity check despite the chain being syntactically valid
wrong: Accept it because any CA-issued certificate authenticates every hostname
Ignore the hostname mismatch if TLS 1.3 is negotiated
Assume Finished automatically fixes the hostname mismatch

questions.prompt: A TLS 1.3 resumed handshake authenticates the peer using a previously established PSK and does not send a new Certificate message. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.correct: Omitting a new certificate can be valid in PSK resumption; authentication relies on the PSK context
wrong: The resumed handshake is necessarily unauthenticated
TLS 1.3 always mandates a new server certificate on resumption
The peer must secretly have negotiated TLS 1.0
